blocks.text: On the eagle's love for its young, from Deut. XXXII, 11.

Now we must speak of the eagle's love for its young. That it is most tender is shown by these words of Moses, Deuter. XXXII, 11: As the eagle stirs up its nest, and hovers over its young, with wings spread out, and taking them carries them upon its feathers. Its nest, that is, its brood: the container for the contained. This manner of speaking is frequent among the Romans. Virgil, in book 4 of the Georgics, says of the bee-eater and the swallow,
They carry in their beaks sweet food to the pitiless nests:

that is, to the cruel chicks, as Servius explains there. Hence Nonius: On the authority of Virgil we may call nidi not only the dwellings of birds but also their offspring. And Columella [col. 177] followed this in his Garden:
And the swallow will have sung the coming of spring to its nests.

So too Solinus on the ibis: It feeds on the eggs of serpents, and brings from them a most welcome food to its nests. And Ammianus, book 22, of the same bird: supplying the eggs of serpents as food to its little nests. Hence the Glosses: Νεοσσὸς [neossos], nidus, chick. And Juvenal, Satire 5, uses it also of children: [II, 760] But now, though your Mygale should give birth, and pour three boys at once into their father's lap, he himself will delight in the chattering nest. — — — —

R. Selomo explains the verb to stir up thus: הזה רחמני על בניו ואינו נכנס לקנו פתאם עד שהוא מקשקש ומטרף על בניו בכנפיו בין אילן לאילן בין שוכה לחברתה כדי שיעורו בניו ויהא בהן כח לקבלו, The eagle, being compassionate towards its young, does not enter its nest abruptly; rather it first makes a noise over them and claps, striking its wings against two trees or against two branches, so that the chicks, thus roused, may have enough strength (that is, may be better prepared) to receive it. To this belongs what follows: על גוזליו ירחף אינו מכביד עצמו עליהם אלא מחופף נוגע ואינו נוגע, It broods over its young (for so he takes the Hebrew ירחף), that is, it does not press its weight on them, but holds itself up so that it touches them as if not touching. Thus he. But Jerome's version, though freer, nevertheless renders the Prophet's meaning much more faithfully: As the eagle, provoking its young to fly, and hovering over them, etc. For the eagle is certainly said to stir up its nest, or its brood, when it provokes it to fly. And the Hebrew רחף means to move oneself, as in Ierem. XXIII, 9. רחפו, All my bones have trembled. So at the creation the Spirit of God מרחפת, was moving to and fro over the face of the waters. From there, transferred to birds, רחף means to move the wings to and fro, as birds do when hovering. From this the Talmudists derived a verb of the same meaning, רפרף, with the guttural elided and the other letters doubled. Hence in the tractate Cholin, fol. 38. b: והעוף אפילו לא רפרף אלא גפו ולא כשכש אלא זנבו הרי זה פירכוס, And a bird, if it only moves its wing, or only wags its tail, this is a convulsive movement. Accordingly in Beresith Rabba the Spirit מרחפת of Gen. I, 3. is said to be כעוף הזה שהוא מרפרף בכנפיו, like that bird which moves its wings to and fro. The Arabs too use the same verb in this way. Alcamus renders it بسط جناحها [basaṭa janāḥahā] It spread out its wings. And the verbal noun الرفرفة [al-rafrafa] is for him الصوت وتحريك الظليم جناحيها حول الشي الذي يريد ان يقع عليه [al-ṣawt wa-taḥrīk al-ẓalīm janāḥayhā ḥawla al-shay al-ladhī yurīdu an yaqaʿa ʿalayhi] The noise and movement of the wings of the ostrich around the thing on which it wishes to alight. Since this is habitual to the ostrich, the bird itself is called رفراف [rafrāf] riphraph. So too another bird, very different from the ostrich, whose other name is خاطف ظله [khāṭif ẓillihi], that is, σκιάρπαξ [skiarpax], snatcher of its own shadow: because, when it sees its image in the water, it flies at it, moving its wings, as if to seize it. Moreover the verb رف [raffa] in the fourth conjugation, that is, ارف [arafa] arappha, is attributed to birds that spread their wings to brood. The same Alcamus: ارفت الدجاجة علي [col. 178] بياضها بسطت الجناح [arafat al-dajāja ʿalā bayāḍihā basaṭat al-janāḥ] Arapphath the hen over her eggs, that is, she spread out her wings, namely in order to brood on them. Yet what we have said is true, [II, 761] that this verb properly signifies a spreading of the wings accompanied by moving them to and fro. This is especially fitting for the eagle, or for any other bird that teaches its still tender chicks their first πτερυγισμοὺς [pterygismous] and ὀρταλισμούς [ortalismous]. Accordingly the Prophet, after ירחף, adds by way of explanation (ἐπεξηγητικῶς [epexēgētikōs]) יפרש כנפיו, it spreads its wings; because the eagle does not move its wings to and fro unless they are spread. Indeed, the movement of the wings is so natural to the eagle that even the chicks constantly flap their wings while eating. So the Arabs report in Damir: ومن عادة هذا الطاير ان يزق كل فرخ ضايع [wa-min ʿādat hādhā al-ṭāyir an yuzaqqa kull farkh ḍāyiʿ] It is also of the nature of this bird that every chick flaps its wings while it is being fed: namely by its mother, beak inserted into beak. For that is properly زق [zaqq].
